What is the most
dangerous long-term
consequence of detonating
a nuclear weapon in space?
In 1962, when the
Starfish Prime warhead
exploded about four hundred
kilometers above the
Pacific, the flash faded
within seconds.
But what it left
behind did not.
The high-energy electrons
released by the blast
did not simply disappear
into the void.
Instead, Earth's magnetic
field acted like an
invisible cage, trapping
huge numbers of charged
particles around our planet.
This created a dense,
man-made radiation belt
that lingered for months,
and in some regions for years.
In the early 1960s,
satellite technology was
in its infancy,
with only a small
number of spacecraft
circling the globe.
Yet in the months
after the detonation,
that trapped radiation
damaged or disabled several
satellites.
Some accounts say about
a third of those
in low Earth orbit,
though the exact count
is uncertain.
Among the casualties was
Telstar, one of the
first communications
satellites.
The trapped electrons
pierced sensitive electronic
circuits and wore down
the early solar panels,
until the spacecraft fell
silent.
Today, the situation is
very different.
We rely on thousands
of satellites for
navigation, banking, weather
forecasting, and
communication.
If a high-altitude nuclear
detonation occurred near
Earth today, scientists
warn the effects on
satellites could be severe
and long lasting.
Exact outcomes are
uncertain, and they would
depend on the weapon,
its altitude, and how
well each satellite is
protected.
That uncertainty is exactly
why a pair of
treaties followed that era.
In 1963, the Partial
Test Ban Treaty banned
nuclear explosions in space,
and in 1967 the
Outer Space Treaty barred
nuclear weapons from orbit.
Think about how little
anyone understood about
this at the time.
Space felt enormous and
empty, as if anything
released there would simply
be lost.
In reality, the planet's
own magnetic field turned
that emptiness into a trap.
One test, one flash,
and a ghostly belt
of radiation around our
planet.
Dive into the full
video to uncover how
fragile our orbital world
truly is.
